content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended reducing sodium intake to levels lower than currently advised, as this could lead to even greater health benefits. Additionally, two recent cohort studies have suggested that reducing sodium intake to less than 2 grams per day may be associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and stroke. The development of this guideline followed WHO's evidence-informed procedures, as outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. The process was led by the WHO Department of Nutrition for Health and Development, in collaboration with the Department of Research Policy and Cooperation and members of the WHO Secretariat. Oversight was provided by the WHO Steering Committee for Nutrition Guideline Development, which included representatives from all relevant WHO departments. Two additional groups were formed: an advisory guideline group and an external expert and stakeholder panel. The WHO Nutrition Guidance Expert Advisory Group (NUGAG) Subgroup on Diet and Health was convened to support the guideline's development. This group included experts from previous WHO advisory panels and others identified through open calls for specialists. No representatives from commercial organizations were included, as WHO prohibits such individuals from participating in guideline groups. External resource persons, including subject matter experts and systematic review methodologists, were invited as observers to provide technical input but did not participate in decision-making. The NUGAG Subgroup advised WHO on selecting important outcomes for decision-making and interpreting evidence. The External Expert and Stakeholder Panel was consulted during the planning stages to define the guideline's scope and research questions. This panel also reviewed and provided feedback on the draft guideline. WHO issued an open call for public comments, and feedback was incorporated into the final guideline. The guideline's development involved systematic reviews and meta-analyses to address specific research questions. These questions were based on the needs of WHO Member States and international partners for policy and program guidance. The Population, Intervention, Control, and Outcomes (PICO) format was used to generate the research questions, which were reviewed by the WHO Secretariat and Steering Committee and made available for public comment. Feedback from stakeholders was used to refine the questions and define the scope of the evidence. The evidence was assessed using the GRADE methodology, which evaluates the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations. The NUGAG Subgroup discussed the evidence and reached a consensus on the recommendations. These findings were consistent with previous reviews. Although the evidence on the effects of reduced sodium intake on cardiovascular disease, stroke, and coronary heart disease was inconclusive, cohort studies showed a significant association between sodium intake and stroke risk. There was no evidence of adverse effects of reduced sodium intake on blood lipids, catecholamine levels, or renal function. In fact, some studies suggested potential benefits for renal function. The findings suggest that reducing sodium intake is beneficial for most individuals, regardless of their current sodium consumption levels. The guideline emphasizes the importance of reducing sodium intake to improve public health outcomes.
